docs.title: Overview
docs.text: minrecord is a minimalist Python library to record values in a ML workflow. A record stores the most recent values (a bounded number of (step, value) pairs) and, for a comparable record, the best value, which is kept even after it leaves the recent values. A record manager groups several records, and every record can be saved to and restored from a dictionary. The logic that defines the best value is customizable with a comparator. minrecord only depends on coola.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• 📊 Track Best Values: Automatically track the best value seen during training
  • 🔄 Recent History: Store only recent values to minimize memory usage
  • ✅ Improvement Detection: Easily check if your model is still improving
  • 🎯 Flexible Comparators: Define custom logic to determine what "better" means
  • 🗂️ Record Manager: Organize and manage multiple metrics efficiently
  • 💾 Serialization: Save and load record states (to_dict, from_dict) for checkpointing
  • 🚀 Minimal Dependencies: Lightweight, with coola as the only dependency
  • 🛡️ Strict by Design: Invalid inputs are rejected when they are received, and a failed call leaves the record unchanged

Below is an example to show how to track the best scalar value when the best value is the maximum value and when the best value is the minimum value.

>>> from minrecord import MaxScalarRecord, MinScalarRecord
>>> record_max = MaxScalarRecord("accuracy")
>>> record_max.update([(0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46)])
>>> record_max.add_value(40)
>>> record_max.get_best_value()
46
>>> record_min = MinScalarRecord("loss")
>>> record_min.update([(0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46)])
>>> record_min.add_value(50)
>>> record_min.get_best_value()
42

docs.title: API stability
docs.text: While minrecord is in development stage, no API is guaranteed to be stable from one release to the next. In fact, it is very likely that the API will change multiple times before a stable 1.0.0 release. In practice, this means that upgrading minrecord to a new version will possibly break any code that was using the old version of minrecord.

docs.title: Design
docs.text: This page explains how minrecord works and why it is built this way. It starts with the model, then lists what every record guarantees, then describes the main design choices with their trade-offs, so you can decide whether they fit your use case. It ends with what the library does not do.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A record is a named, bounded sequence of pairs (step, value). The step is a label that says when the value was added (an epoch, an iteration, or None). A record keeps the last max_size pairs, called the recent values, and drops the oldest one when it is full.

A comparable record (ComparableRecord, MinScalarRecord, MaxScalarRecord) also keeps the best pair (step, value), apart from the recent values. A comparator decides if a new value is better than the best one. A manager (RecordManager) stores records by key and works on all of them.

BaseRecord ── Record ── ComparableRecord ── MinScalarRecord / MaxScalarRecord
                              │
                         BaseComparator ── MinScalarComparator / MaxScalarComparator
RecordManager: {key: BaseRecord}

Every record is rebuilt from one snapshot: to_dict() returns the arguments of the constructor (and the full name of the class under _target_), content included. from_dict, clone, equal and load_dict are all defined from this snapshot.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
These guarantees come from the base classes, so every record has them.

Guarantee Statement Bounded memory A record keeps at most max_size pairs, with 1 <= max_size <= sys.maxsize. The oldest pair is dropped first. Adding a value is O(1). Best is never lost The best pair of a comparable record is stored apart from the recent values: it survives the eviction of the pair that produced it, clone and to_dict/from_dict. No sentinel An empty comparable record has no best pair (None). inf and -inf are never used as a stand-in. Ties improve A value equal to the best value counts as an improvement. The comparison is reflexive: is_better(new_value=x, old_value=x) is True for all x, NaN included. NaN never wins A NaN is never better than a number. A NaN best value is replaced by any value (a number, or another NaN as a tie). Exact round trip For every record r, also after a JSON round trip and when it holds NaN: BaseRecord.from_dict(r.to_dict()).equal(r) and r.clone().equal(r). The clone has the same has_improved() and the same best pair, and it is independent. Consistent state A comparable record has a best pair if and only if it has a value. Safe loading from_dict, load_dict, load_state_dict and the comparator dict only build objects of the expected type, and anything that is not a dict is a TypeError. Fails early An input that cannot work is rejected by the call that receives it and is never stored: a value that the comparator cannot compare, an invalid max_size, a name that is not a str, an unknown manager key. Atomic add_value, load_dict and RecordManager.load_state_dict leave the record, or the manager, unchanged if they raise. update is a loop of add_value: the elements before the failing one are kept. Typed errors EmptyRecordError, NotAComparableRecordError, ValueError (max_size, best), TypeError (name, dict or comparator of the wrong type), KeyError (unknown manager key). Readable text repr and str of records and comparators are deterministic and show the arguments (no memory address). Consistent with coola Records, comparators and managers work with objects_are_equal, and to_dict works with coola.factory.factory. Minimal One dependency (coola), no optional dependency, no I/O, no logging, no thread, and no global state beyond the default max_size.

docs.title: Bounded window, best value stored apart
docs.text:
A training job can add values for millions of steps, and the loggers (MLflow, TensorBoard, ...) do not give back the last or the best value. A record keeps a small window, and the best pair separately.

  • Benefit: constant memory, O(1) add_value, and the best value is exact even after its pair has left the window.
  • Cost: the history is not complete. If you need all the values (to plot a curve for example), send them to a logger, or use a larger max_size. max_size is fixed when the record is created: to change it, create a new record and transfer the values with new.update(old.get_most_recent()) (the best value is then recomputed from the window only; use best= to keep it).

docs.title: Ties count as improvements
docs.text:
has_improved() is True when the last value is equal to the best value, so a metric that stays at its optimum keeps improving, and a checkpoint is saved at each step of the plateau.

  • Benefit: the comparison is reflexive, which a record needs to be rebuilt from to_dict (replaying the last value against a best value that is that value gives the same flag). get_best_step is the latest step among the ties.
  • Cost: code that saves a checkpoint only on a strict improvement must compare the values itself. A custom comparator must use >= or <=, not > or <.

docs.title: One snapshot rebuilds an object
docs.text:
to_dict() is exactly the arguments of the constructor. There is no separate configuration and state, and no registry: the class is found from _target_.

  • Benefit: clone, equal, from_dict and load_dict are final methods of the base class, so a custom record only implements six members and gets them right. improved is derived from the values and never stored, so a snapshot cannot be inconsistent.
  • Cost: equal is the equality of the snapshots, so it needs the values to be comparable by coola, and a NaN is equal to a NaN even with objects_are_equal(..., equal_nan=False). This is the one deliberate difference with coola: it lets a record that holds a NaN be equal to its JSON round trip. The state of a custom record must live in vars(self) (no __slots__), because load_dict replaces it.

docs.title: The first value is compared with itself
docs.text:
The first value of a comparable record is the best value, and it goes through the comparator like any other value.

  • Benefit: a value that the comparator cannot compare (None, a string, 10**400) is rejected by the add_value that receives it, and the record stays empty. A comparator needs no initial value.
  • Cost: the comparator must be reflexive, which is a rule of BaseComparator.

docs.title: Loading only builds the expected type
docs.text:
BaseRecord.from_dict(data) imports the object named by _target_ and checks that it is a record class before calling it. MinScalarRecord.from_dict only accepts a MinScalarRecord (or a subclass), BaseRecord.from_dict accepts any record, and a _target_ inside a stored value is data that is never instantiated.

  • Benefit: a dict cannot make the library call an arbitrary importable function, and loading the wrong type is an error and not a silent change of type.
  • Cost: the module named by _target_ is still imported, so do not load a dict from an untrusted source without checking _target_.

docs.title: load_dict replaces the whole state
docs.text:
record.load_dict(data) builds a new record first, then replaces vars(record). The record is not changed if the dict is invalid or has another type.

  • Benefit: the objects that other parts of your code hold are updated (a trainer that keeps a reference to a record, for example), and the loaded state is exactly the saved one.
  • Cost: the name and the max_size are replaced too. A record named a that loads the dict of a record named b is named b. Check the name before if it must stay.

docs.title: Strict manager, with an opt-in factory
docs.text:
RecordManager.get_record(key) raises KeyError for a key that nobody registered. To create the records on demand, pass a default_factory (as for collections.defaultdict): it is called with the key and returns the record.

  • Benefit: a typo in a metric name is reported, instead of silently storing the values in a record that nobody reads. The factory also chooses the type, so on-demand records can have a best value (RecordManager(default_factory=MinScalarRecord)).
  • Cost: one more line of setup when you want on-demand records. The factory is not part of the state: state_dict, equal and load_state_dict do not use it.

docs.title: load_state_dict merges
docs.text:
The state of a manager is merged into it: the data of a known key is loaded in the existing record, the records of the new keys are created, and a record that the state does not mention is kept. All the entries are built and checked first, so the manager is not modified if one entry is invalid.

  • Cost: an entry of a known key is built twice (once to check it, once to load it), which is one more constructor call on at most max_size pairs. A manager that must match a checkpoint exactly should be created empty before loading.

docs.title: Validation at the boundary
docs.text: max_size, name, best and dictionaries are validated by the call that receives them, with the most specific exception. The only global setting is the default max_size (get_max_size, set_max_size, reset_max_size), which is read when a record is created, so changing it does not affect the existing records.

docs.title: Extending the library
docs.text:
• A new notion of "better": implement BaseComparator.is_better(*, new_value, old_value) and use it with ComparableRecord. If the comparator has arguments, override to_dict (for example {**super().to_dict(), "tolerance": self._tolerance}) so the record can be saved and loaded. See the custom comparator example.
  • A new type of record: implement the six abstract members of BaseRecord (name, add_value, get_last_value, get_most_recent, is_empty, to_dict). to_dict must return what the constructor accepts, with _target_. Override is_comparable, get_best_value, get_best_step and has_improved if the record can compare values.

docs.title: Not guaranteed
docs.text:
• Thread safety. A record and a manager are not thread-safe. Use one record per thread, or a lock.
  • Values are stored by reference. add_value does not copy the value, and to_dict and clone share the value objects with the original. Store scalars or immutable objects.
  • Order of the steps. step is a label: it is not checked to increase, nor to be a number. Early stopping with get_best_step needs a numeric step.
  • Truthiness. Record and RecordManager define __len__, so an empty one is falsy: write record.is_empty(), not if record:.
  • copy.copy(record) is not a clone. A shallow copy shares the recent values, so add_value on the copy changes the original. Use clone() (or copy.deepcopy).
  • Stability of the API. The API is not stable before 1.0.0 (see the release notes).

docs.title: What is minrecord?
docs.text: minrecord is a minimalist Python library designed to record and track values in machine learning workflows. It helps you track the best values, monitor recent metrics, and determine if your models are improving.

docs.title: Why use minrecord instead of storing values in a list?
docs.text:
While you can use a list, minrecord provides:

  • Memory efficiency: Only stores recent values (configurable)
  • Best value tracking: Automatically tracks the best value even if it's no longer in the recent history
  • Improvement detection: Easy to check if the latest value improved
  • Structured management: RecordManager helps organize multiple metrics
  • Serialization: Built-in support for saving/loading state

docs.title: Is minrecord only for machine learning?
docs.text:
No! While designed with ML in mind, minrecord can be used anywhere you need to track:

  • Best values over time
  • Recent measurements
  • Whether metrics are improving

docs.title: How do I install minrecord?
docs.text: pip install minrecord

docs.title: What Python versions are supported?
docs.text: Python 3.11 and higher are officially supported.

docs.title: Do I need PyTorch or other ML frameworks?
docs.text: No, minrecord has minimal dependencies. It only requires coola, which is used for equality, string formatting and the creation of objects from a dictionary.

docs.title: When should I use Record vs ComparableRecord?
docs.text:
• Use Record when you only need to track recent values
  • Use ComparableRecord/MinScalarRecord/MaxScalarRecord when you need to:
  • Track the best value
  • Check if values are improving
  • Implement early stopping

docs.title: How do I choose max_size?
docs.text:
Consider:

  • Small values (10-50): For simple monitoring during training
  • Large values (100-1000): For detailed analysis or plotting trends
  • Memory constraints: Larger max_size × number of records × value size

Default is 10, which works well for most ML training scenarios.

docs.title: Can I change max_size after creating a record?
docs.text:
No, max_size is fixed at creation. If you need to change it:

  1. Create a new record with the desired max_size
  2. Transfer the values using new_record.update(old_record.get_most_recent()). The best value is recomputed from the transferred values only: to keep a best value that has left the recent values, pass it with best=(old_record.get_best_step(), old_record.get_best_value()) (it requires elements).

Changing the default with set_max_size only affects the records created afterwards.

docs.title: What happens when the record is full?
docs.text: The oldest value is automatically removed when adding a new value. The record uses a deque internally with a fixed maximum length.

docs.title: Can I create a record from some values?
docs.text:
Yes, pass them with elements. They are added with add_value, so the best value and has_improved() are correct, and only the last max_size elements are kept:

record = MinScalarRecord("loss", elements=[(0, 1.5), (1, 1.3)])

If the best value is not in the elements anymore (for example when a record is resumed), pass it with best=(step, value). best must be a pair and it requires at least one element (ValueError otherwise), because a record has a best value if and only if it has a value. Use to_dict() and BaseRecord.from_dict() to save and resume a record: the best value is included.

docs.title: How does has_improved() work?
docs.text:
has_improved() returns True if the last added value is equal to or better than the best value seen so far.

record = MinScalarRecord("loss")
record.add_value(1.5)
record.has_improved()  # True (first value is always improvement)

record.add_value(1.3)
record.has_improved()  # True (1.3 < 1.5)

record.add_value(1.4)
record.has_improved()  # False (1.4 > 1.3)

docs.title: What happens with NaN values?
docs.text:
A NaN value is never better than a number, so it never becomes the best value when a number exists. A NaN best value is replaced by any value: the first number, or another NaN (a tie). The first value of a record is always the best value, even if it is NaN. Two records that hold the same NaN values are equal (equal treats NaN as equal to NaN), also after a JSON round trip.

record = MinScalarRecord("loss")
record.add_value(float("nan"))
record.add_value(1.5)
record.get_best_value()  # 1.5
record.add_value(float("nan"))
record.get_best_value()  # 1.5

docs.title: Why does has_improved() return True for equal values?
docs.text: By design, equal values are considered improvements. This is useful when a metric plateaus at the optimal value, and it is required to rebuild a record exactly from to_dict() (see Design). If you only want to act on a strict improvement, compare the new value with the previous best value before adding it.

docs.title: Can I create custom comparators?
docs.text:
Yes! Implement BaseComparator, it has only one abstract method. The first value of a record is always the best value, so a comparator does not need an initial value. A new value that is equal to the old value must be better (the comparison is reflexive: is_better(new_value=x, old_value=x) is True for every x), so a plateau counts as an improvement and a record can be rebuilt from its to_dict output:

from minrecord.comparator import BaseComparator


class MyComparator(BaseComparator[float]):
    def is_better(self, *, new_value: float, old_value: float) -> bool:
        # Define your comparison logic
        return new_value >= old_value

If your comparator has some arguments, override to_dict() so the record can be saved and loaded ({**super().to_dict(), "tolerance": self._tolerance}).

docs.title: What's the benefit of RecordManager?
docs.text:
RecordManager provides:

  • Organized storage: All records in one place
  • Convenience methods: get_best_values(), get_last_values()
  • State management: Save/load all records together

docs.title: Does RecordManager create records automatically?
docs.text:
No, not by default. get_record() raises a KeyError for a key that nobody registered, so a typo in a metric name is reported instead of storing the values in a record that nobody reads. To create the missing records on demand, pass a default_factory (as for collections.defaultdict). It is called with the key and returns the record:

from minrecord import MinScalarRecord, Record, RecordManager

manager = RecordManager(default_factory=Record)
record = manager.get_record("new_metric")  # A Record named "new_metric"

# A best value for every new metric:
manager = RecordManager(default_factory=MinScalarRecord)

The default_factory is not part of the state: state_dict(), equal() and load_state_dict() do not use it.

To check if a record exists first:

if manager.has_record("my_metric"):
    record = manager.get_record("my_metric")

docs.title: Can I use different record types in the same manager?
docs.text:
Yes! RecordManager accepts any BaseRecord implementation:

manager = RecordManager()
manager.add_record(MinScalarRecord("loss"))
manager.add_record(MaxScalarRecord("accuracy"))
manager.add_record(Record("custom_metric"))

docs.title: How do I save and resume a record or a manager?
docs.text: Use to_dict() / BaseRecord.from_dict() for a record and state_dict() / load_state_dict() for a manager. The dictionaries can be written to JSON. See the usage guide and the design choices.

docs.title: How do I implement early stopping?
docs.text: Use get_best_step(): it is the step of the best value, also when the pair has left the recent values. See Pattern 3 of the usage guide. It needs a numeric step.

docs.title: What is EmptyRecordError?
docs.text:
This error occurs when you try to get a value from an empty record:

record = Record("my_metric")
# record.get_last_value()  # Raises EmptyRecordError

# Check first
if not record.is_empty():
    value = record.get_last_value()

docs.title: What is NotAComparableRecordError?
docs.text:
This error occurs when you call comparison methods on a non-comparable record:

record = Record("my_metric")  # Not comparable
# record.get_best_value()  # Raises NotAComparableRecordError

# Use is_comparable() to check
if record.is_comparable():
    best = record.get_best_value()

docs.title: How many records can I have?
docs.text:
There's no hard limit. Each record has minimal overhead. With max_size=10:

  • Memory per record: about 1 KB when empty, and about 3 KB for a MinScalarRecord that holds 10 (step, float) pairs (measured with tracemalloc on Python 3.14; it depends on the Python version and on the values)
  • 1000 records with 10 scalars each: about 3 MB

docs.title: Is minrecord thread-safe?
docs.text:
No, records and managers are not thread-safe. If using multiple threads:

  • Use separate records per thread, or
  • Implement your own locking mechanism

docs.title: Can I use minrecord in distributed training?
docs.text:
Yes, but each process needs its own records. After training:

  • Gather metrics from all processes
  • Aggregate as needed for logging

docs.title: How do I integrate with TensorBoard?
docs.text:
from torch.utils.tensorboard import SummaryWriter
from minrecord import Record, RecordManager

writer = SummaryWriter()
manager = RecordManager(default_factory=Record)

for epoch in range(epochs):
    # Training...
    # Add values to records
    for name, value in metrics.items():
        manager.get_record(name).add_value(value, step=epoch)

    # Log to TensorBoard
    for name in manager.get_records().keys():
        record = manager.get_record(name)
        if not record.is_empty():
            writer.add_scalar(name, record.get_last_value(), epoch)

docs.title: How do I integrate with Weights & Biases (wandb)?
docs.text:
import wandb
from minrecord import Record, RecordManager

wandb.init(project="my-project")
manager = RecordManager(default_factory=Record)

for epoch in range(epochs):
    # Training...
    # Add values to records
    for name, value in metrics.items():
        manager.get_record(name).add_value(value, step=epoch)

    wandb.log(
        {
            "epoch": epoch,
            **manager.get_last_values(prefix="train/"),
            **manager.get_best_values(prefix="best/"),
        }
    )

docs.title: Does minrecord work with PyTorch Lightning?
docs.text:
Yes! Use records in your LightningModule (PyTorch Lightning 2.x). Log the validation loss with self.log in validation_step, then read it in on_validation_epoch_end:

import pytorch_lightning as pl
from minrecord import MinScalarRecord


class MyModel(pl.LightningModule):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.val_loss = MinScalarRecord("val_loss")

    def on_validation_epoch_end(self):
        loss = self.trainer.callback_metrics["val_loss"].item()
        self.val_loss.add_value(loss, step=self.current_epoch)

        if self.val_loss.has_improved():
            self.trainer.save_checkpoint("best_model.ckpt")

docs.title: Values seem incorrect after loading state
docs.text:
Load the whole dict returned by to_dict() (it contains the best value and the recent values), or create the record from its values:

# Correct
record = BaseRecord.from_dict(state)

# Also correct
record = MinScalarRecord("loss", elements=elements)

docs.title: get_best_values() returns fewer items than expected
docs.text:
get_best_values() only returns values for:

  • Non-empty records
  • Comparable records

Use get_last_values() for all records:

last_values = manager.get_last_values()  # All non-empty records
best_values = manager.get_best_values()  # Only comparable records

docs.title: Record not found errors
docs.text:
get_record() raises a KeyError that lists the known keys when no record is registered for the key. Check that record names match exactly:

manager.add_record(MinScalarRecord("train/loss"))  # Note the "/"
# Wrong name:
manager.get_record("train_loss").add_value(1.5, step=0)  # KeyError: No record is registered ...
# Correct:
manager.get_record("train/loss").add_value(1.5, step=0)

If you want the records to be created on demand, use RecordManager(default_factory=...).

docs.title: Get Started
docs.text: It is highly recommended to install in a virtual environment to keep your system in order.

docs.title: Installing with pip or uv pip (recommended)
docs.text:
The following command installs the latest version of the library:

# pip
pip install minrecord

# uv
uv pip install minrecord

minrecord has no optional dependency: only coola is installed with it.

docs.title: Installing from source
docs.text:
To install minrecord from source, you can follow the steps below. First, you will need to install uv. uv is used to manage and install the dependencies. If uv is already installed on your machine, you can skip this step. You can install uv by running:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

You can check the uv installation by running the following command:

uv --version

Then, you can clone the git repository:

git clone git@github.com:durandtibo/minrecord.git
cd minrecord

It is recommended to create a Python 3.11+ virtual environment. This step is optional so you can skip it. You can use uv to create a virtual environment:

make setup-venv
source .venv/bin/activate

This example uses uv to create a virtual environment, but you can use other tools or configurations. Then, you should install the required package to use minrecord with the following command:

inv env.install

This command installs all the required packages (and inv env.update updates them). Finally, you can test the installation with the following command:

inv test.unit --cov

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This page gives a quick overview on how to use the minrecord. You should read this page if you want to learn how to use the records. This page does not explain the internal behavior of the records: see the design page. While minrecord was designed to work in a ML workflow, you can use it in other contexts if it fits your need.

Prerequisites: You’ll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial.

docs.title: Record
docs.text:
minrecord is organized around the BaseRecord class. It defines the interface to implement a record object. minrecord provides the Record class, which is a generic implementation of a record. Each Record object has a name and tracks the last values.

>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("loss")
>>> record
Record(name=loss, max_size=10, size=0)
>>> record.name
'loss'

Usually, it is useful to keep only the last values. It is also possible to track a large number of values, but it can consume a lot of memory if the values to track take a significant amount of memory. By default, the Record objects only track the last 10 values, but it is possible to control the memory consumption by setting carefully the max_size argument.

>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("my_record", max_size=5)
>>> record
Record(name=my_record, max_size=5, size=0)

After creating a record, the add_value method can be used to add a value to the record. The following example shows how to add the value 4.2 to the record.

>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("loss")
>>> record.add_value(4.2)
>>> record
Record(name=loss, max_size=10, size=1)

When adding a value, it is possible to specify a step to track when the value was added.

>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("loss")
>>> record.add_value(4.2, step=2)
>>> record
Record(name=loss, max_size=10, size=1)

The step can be a number or None. None means no valid step to track. It is possible to get the last value added by using the get_last_value method.

>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("loss")
>>> record.add_value(4.2, step=1)
>>> record.add_value(2.4, step=2)
>>> record
Record(name=loss, max_size=10, size=2)
>>> record.get_last_value()
2.4

Calling get_last_value on an empty record raises an EmptyRecordError exception. It is possible to check if a record is empty or not by using the is_empty method.

>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("loss")
>>> record.is_empty()
True
>>> record.add_value(4.2, step=1)
>>> record.is_empty()
False

If there are multiple values to add, it is possible to use the update method. The input is a sequence of 2-tuples where the first item is the step and the second item is the value.

>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("loss")
>>> record.update([(0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46)])
>>> record
Record(name=loss, max_size=10, size=3)
>>> record.get_last_value()
46

In the example above, the second element does not have a valid step so the value is set to None. It is possible to add elements when creating the record.

>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("loss", elements=[(0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46)])
>>> record
Record(name=loss, max_size=10, size=3)
>>> record.get_last_value()
46

It is possible to access the most recent values added to the record by using the get_most_recent method.

>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("loss", elements=[(0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46)])
>>> record.add_value(40)
>>> record.get_most_recent()
((0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46), (None, 40))

The max_size argument is optional: if it is not given, the default maximum size is used. It can be read with get_max_size, changed with set_max_size and restored with reset_max_size. A change only affects the records created after it.

>>> from minrecord import Record, get_max_size, reset_max_size, set_max_size
>>> get_max_size()
10
>>> set_max_size(3)
>>> Record("loss")
Record(name=loss, max_size=3, size=0)
>>> reset_max_size()
>>> Record("loss")
Record(name=loss, max_size=10, size=0)

It is possible to check if two Record objects are equal by calling the equal method.

>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record1 = Record("loss")
>>> record2 = Record("loss", elements=[(0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46)])
>>> record3 = Record("loss", elements=[(0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46)])
>>> record1.equal(record2)
False
>>> record3.equal(record2)
True

docs.title: Comparable Record
docs.text:
minrecord also provides some comparable records i.e. records that track the best value. There is a generic ComparableRecord class where the user just needs to implement the comparator object that is used to find the best value. There are MaxScalarRecord and MinScalarRecord that are specialized implementations of ComparableRecord for scalars (e.g. float or int). It is possible to know if a record is comparable by calling the is_comparable methods.

>>> from minrecord import MaxScalarRecord, MinScalarRecord, Record
>>> record = Record("my_value")
>>> record.is_comparable()
False
>>> record_max = MaxScalarRecord("accuracy")
>>> record_max.is_comparable()
True
>>> record_min = MinScalarRecord("loss")
>>> record_min.is_comparable()
True

These records support the Record functionalities, and additional functionalities. It is possible to use the get_best_value method to get the best value.

>>> from minrecord import MaxScalarRecord, MinScalarRecord
>>> record_max = MaxScalarRecord("accuracy")
>>> record_max.update([(0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46)])
>>> record_max.add_value(40)
>>> record_max.get_best_value()
46
>>> record_min = MinScalarRecord("loss")
>>> record_min.update([(0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46)])
>>> record_min.add_value(50)
>>> record_min.get_best_value()
42

The record tracks the best value even if the best value is not stored in the record. Below is an example where the record's maximum size is set to 3.

>>> from minrecord import MinScalarRecord
>>> record = MinScalarRecord("loss", max_size=3)
>>> record.update([(0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46)])
>>> record.add_value(50)
>>> record.add_value(60)
>>> record.get_most_recent()
((2, 46), (None, 50), (None, 60))
>>> record.get_best_value()
42

The get_best_step method returns the step of the best value, even if the pair that produced it is not in the recent values anymore. If several values are equal to the best value, it is the latest step. It is useful to know which epoch was the best one, for example to load the best checkpoint.

>>> from minrecord import MinScalarRecord
>>> record = MinScalarRecord("loss", max_size=2)
>>> record.update([(0, 42), (1, 45), (2, 46), (3, 50)])
>>> record.get_best_step()
0

Calling get_best_value or get_best_step on an empty record raises an EmptyRecordError exception. It is possible to know if the last value added improved the best value or not by calling the has_improved method.

>>> from minrecord import MinScalarRecord
>>> record = MinScalarRecord("loss")
>>> record.add_value(50)
>>> record.has_improved()
True
>>> record.add_value(60)
>>> record.has_improved()
False
>>> record.add_value(42)
>>> record.has_improved()
True
>>> record.add_value(43)
>>> record.has_improved()
False

By definition, has_improved will return True if the last value is equal to the best value as shown in the example below.

>>> from minrecord import MinScalarRecord
>>> record = MinScalarRecord("loss")
>>> record.add_value(42)
>>> record.has_improved()
True
>>> record.add_value(42)
>>> record.has_improved()
True

Calling has_improved or get_best_value on non-comparable record raises a NotAComparableRecordError exception. This is also the case for get_best_step.

The elements argument of the constructor adds the values with add_value, so the best value and has_improved are correct when a record is created from some elements.

>>> from minrecord import MinScalarRecord
>>> record = MinScalarRecord("loss", elements=[(0, 42), (None, 45), (2, 46)])
>>> record.add_value(50)
>>> record.get_best_value()
42

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
to_dict returns the arguments of the constructor, so a record can be saved (for example in a JSON file) and rebuilt with BaseRecord.from_dict. The best value is kept even if it is not in the recent values.

>>> import json
>>> from minrecord import BaseRecord, MinScalarRecord
>>> record = MinScalarRecord("loss", max_size=2, elements=[(0, 1.0), (1, 5.0), (2, 6.0)])
>>> data = json.loads(json.dumps(record.to_dict()))
>>> new_record = BaseRecord.from_dict(data)
>>> new_record.equal(record)
True
>>> new_record.get_best_value()
1.0

from_dict only builds a record of the expected type: MinScalarRecord.from_dict raises a TypeError for the dict of another type of record. The load_dict method loads a dictionary in an existing record, in place. It replaces the whole state of the record, the name and the max_size included, and it does not change the record if the dictionary is invalid.

>>> from minrecord import MinScalarRecord
>>> record = MinScalarRecord("loss")
>>> record.load_dict(MinScalarRecord("loss", elements=[(0, 1.5)]).to_dict())
>>> record.get_best_value()
1.5

clone returns an independent copy of a record (the values are shared, not copied).

docs.title: Custom Comparator
docs.text:
A ComparableRecord uses a comparator to find the best value. A comparator implements one method, is_better. A value that is equal to the best value must be better, so use >= or <= and not > or <.

>>> from minrecord import BaseComparator, ComparableRecord
>>> class AbsMinComparator(BaseComparator[float]):
...     def is_better(self, *, new_value: float, old_value: float) -> bool:
...         return abs(new_value) <= abs(old_value)
>>> record = ComparableRecord("error", AbsMinComparator())
>>> record.update([(0, -3.0), (1, 2.0), (2, -2.5)])
>>> record.get_best_value()
2.0

docs.title: Record Manager
docs.text:
When working with multiple records, RecordManager provides a convenient way to organize and manage them. It allows you to add, update, and query multiple records efficiently.

>>> from minrecord import RecordManager, MinScalarRecord, MaxScalarRecord
>>> manager = RecordManager()
>>> manager.add_record(MinScalarRecord("loss"))
>>> manager.add_record(MaxScalarRecord("accuracy"))
>>> manager
RecordManager(
  (loss): MinScalarRecord(name=loss, max_size=10, size=0)
  (accuracy): MaxScalarRecord(name=accuracy, max_size=10, size=0)
)

You can update multiple records at once:

>>> from minrecord import RecordManager, MinScalarRecord, MaxScalarRecord
>>> manager = RecordManager()
>>> manager.add_record(MinScalarRecord("loss"))
>>> manager.add_record(MaxScalarRecord("accuracy"))
>>> manager.get_record("loss").add_value(1.5, step=0)
>>> manager.get_record("accuracy").add_value(0.85, step=0)
>>> manager.get_record("loss").add_value(1.3, step=1)
>>> manager.get_record("accuracy").add_value(0.87, step=1)
>>> manager.get_record("loss").get_best_value()
1.3
>>> manager.get_record("accuracy").get_best_value()
0.87

get_record raises a KeyError if no record is registered for the key. Pass a default_factory, a function of the key that returns a record, to create the missing records on demand:

>>> from minrecord import RecordManager, MinScalarRecord
>>> manager = RecordManager(default_factory=MinScalarRecord)
>>> manager.has_record("loss")
False
>>> manager.get_record("loss")
MinScalarRecord(name=loss, max_size=10, size=0)
>>> manager.has_record("loss")
True

The manager provides convenient methods to get all best or last values:

>>> from minrecord import RecordManager, MinScalarRecord, MaxScalarRecord
>>> manager = RecordManager()
>>> manager.add_record(MinScalarRecord("loss"))
>>> manager.add_record(MaxScalarRecord("accuracy"))
>>> manager.get_record("loss").add_value(1.5, step=0)
>>> manager.get_record("accuracy").add_value(0.85, step=0)
>>> manager.get_record("loss").add_value(1.3, step=1)
>>> manager.get_record("accuracy").add_value(0.87, step=1)
>>> manager.get_best_values()
{'loss': 1.3, 'accuracy': 0.87}
>>> manager.get_last_values(prefix="last/")
{'last/loss': 1.3, 'last/accuracy': 0.87}

The records of a manager are saved with state_dict and restored with load_state_dict. The same computations are available for any mapping of records with the functions get_best_values and get_last_values.

>>> from minrecord import RecordManager, MinScalarRecord
>>> manager = RecordManager({"loss": MinScalarRecord("loss", elements=[(0, 1.5)])})
>>> new_manager = RecordManager()
>>> new_manager.load_state_dict(manager.state_dict())
>>> new_manager.equal(manager)
True

docs.text: This release simplifies the design of the records and has breaking changes. The API is not stable yet (see API stability), so there is no deprecation period and no compatibility layer. The design page explains the current behavior.

docs.title: Migrating from 0.3
docs.text:
Before Now record.config_dict(), record.state_dict(), record.load_state_dict(...) record.to_dict(), BaseRecord.from_dict(data) (new record), record.load_dict(data) (in place) {"config": ..., "state": ...} One flat dict: _target_, name, max_size, elements and, for a comparable record, comparator and best MinScalarRecord.from_elements(name, elements) MinScalarRecord(name, elements=elements) best_value=..., improved=... best=(step, value) (a pair, with at least one element). has_improved() is derived from the values record.is_better(...) comparator.is_better(new_value=..., old_value=...) BaseComparator.get_initial_best_value Removed: the first value of a record is the best value BaseRecord._get_best_value, _has_improved hooks Override get_best_value, get_best_step, has_improved and is_comparable manager.get_record("new") created a Record KeyError. Use RecordManager(default_factory=Record) (or another record class) to create records on demand minrecord.config.Config, get_default_config get_max_size, set_max_size, reset_max_size minrecord.utils.value.MutableValue Removed

The checkpoints of the previous versions are not read.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
Records:

  • elements, max_size and best of Record, ComparableRecord, MaxScalarRecord and MinScalarRecord are keyword-only.
  • best must be a tuple or a list of length 2 and requires elements, otherwise ValueError.
  • BaseRecord has 6 abstract members (name, add_value, get_last_value, get_most_recent, is_empty, to_dict). clone, equal, update, from_dict and load_dict are @final.
  • The first value of a comparable record is compared with itself, so a value that the comparator cannot compare (None, a string, 10**400) is rejected by the add_value that receives it (TypeError or OverflowError, from the comparator) and the record stays empty.
  • Record(name) raises TypeError if name is not a str.
  • An invalid max_size (not a positive int, a bool, or larger than sys.maxsize) raises ValueError.
  • equal requires the same type. The equality of records, comparators and managers is the equality of their snapshot (to_dict, state_dict), and a NaN is equal to a NaN, also with objects_are_equal(..., equal_nan=False).
  • BaseRecord.from_dict returns Self and raises TypeError if _target_ is missing or is not the class (or a subclass of the class) that it is called on. load_dict and RecordManager.load_state_dict raise TypeError for a dict that is not the dict of a record, or that is the dict of another type of record.

Comparators:

  • BaseComparator has one abstract method, is_better(*, new_value, old_value), which is keyword-only. to_dict and equal are concrete: a comparator with arguments overrides to_dict.
  • The comparison must be reflexive: is_better(new_value=x, old_value=x) is True for every x. A custom comparator that is strict (> or <) breaks this contract: use >= or <=.
  • A NaN is never better than a number, and a NaN best value is replaced by any value.
  • BaseComparator has a repr built from to_dict, so str(record) does not contain a memory address.
  • The comparator of ComparableRecord must be a BaseComparator or its dict, otherwise TypeError.

Manager and functions:

  • exist_ok (RecordManager.add_record), and prefix and suffix (RecordManager.get_best_values, get_best_values, get_last_values) are keyword-only.
  • RecordManager(records) copies the mapping.
  • RecordManager.get_record(key) raises KeyError for a key that nobody registered. The new keyword-only default_factory argument creates the records on demand. The factory is not part of the state.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• set_max_size changes the maximum size of the records created after the call (the default was evaluated at import), and a value larger than sys.maxsize is rejected.
  • clone() works for MaxScalarRecord and MinScalarRecord.
  • A falsy best value (0.0) is kept, and the best value of a record created from some elements is correct.
  • get_best_value of an empty record raises EmptyRecordError instead of returning inf or -inf.
  • A comparator that raises in add_value leaves the record unchanged.
  • RecordManager.load_state_dict does not change the manager if an entry is invalid.
  • A configuration that is not a dict raises TypeError (it was AttributeError).
  • has_improved() of a rebuilt record (from_dict, clone) is the one of the original, also when its first value is NaN.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• get_best_step() returns the step of the best value (the latest step among the ties), also if the pair is not in the recent values anymore.
  • RecordManager.get_last_values and RecordManager.equal.
  • reset_max_size is exported at the root of the package.
  • minrecord.utils.validation.check_max_size and check_name, and minrecord.utils.factory.instantiate(config, cls).
  • ComparableRecord accepts the comparator as an object or as its dict.
  • The design page lists the guarantees and the design choices.

docs.title: Usage Guide
docs.text: This guide provides practical information for using minrecord effectively in your projects.

docs.title: When to Use minrecord
docs.text:
minrecord is designed for scenarios where you need to:

  • Track the best value achieved during training (e.g., best validation accuracy)
  • Monitor recent values without storing the entire history
  • Manage multiple metrics in a structured way
  • Determine if your model is still improving
  • Implement early stopping based on metric improvements

docs.title: Records vs Comparable Records
docs.text:
Records (Record) are the basic building blocks that store recent values:

  • Store a configurable number of recent values
  • Provide access to the most recent value
  • Don't track "best" values

Comparable Records (ComparableRecord, MinScalarRecord, MaxScalarRecord) extend records with comparison logic:

  • Track the best value seen so far
  • Indicate whether the latest value is an improvement
  • Use comparators to define what "better" means

docs.title: Memory Management
docs.text:
By default, records keep only the last 10 values. This is configurable, per record or for the records created afterwards (reset_max_size() restores the default):

from minrecord import Record, get_max_size, set_max_size

# Check default
print(get_max_size())  # 10

# Change the default of the records created after this call
set_max_size(20)

# Or set per record
record = Record("my_metric", max_size=50)

Why limit stored values?

  • Reduces memory footprint in long-running training jobs
  • Best values are tracked separately and never lost
  • Recent values are usually sufficient for monitoring

max_size is fixed when the record is created. To change it, create a new record and add the values of the old one (new.update(old.get_most_recent())).

docs.title: Guarantees and Limits
docs.text:
Every record keeps at most max_size values, keeps the best pair apart from them, is rebuilt exactly from to_dict, and rejects invalid inputs in the call that receives them. The design page lists the guarantees, explains the design choices with their trade-offs, and describes what is not guaranteed (thread safety, values stored by reference, copy.copy, ...).

Three points are worth knowing before you start:

  • A value that equals the best value is an improvement. has_improved() is True on a plateau.
  • A NaN is never better than a number. It can only be the best value if it is the first one.
  • An empty record is falsy. Write record.is_empty(), not if record:.

docs.title: Pattern 1: Basic Training Loop
docs.text:
from minrecord import MinScalarRecord, MaxScalarRecord

train_loss = MinScalarRecord("train_loss")
val_accuracy = MaxScalarRecord("val_accuracy")

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    # Training...
    train_loss.add_value(epoch_loss, step=epoch)
    val_accuracy.add_value(epoch_acc, step=epoch)

    if val_accuracy.has_improved():
        save_checkpoint(model, "best_model.pt")

docs.title: Pattern 2: Managing Multiple Metrics
docs.text:
from minrecord import RecordManager, MinScalarRecord, MaxScalarRecord

manager = RecordManager()
manager.add_record(MinScalarRecord("train/loss"))
manager.add_record(MinScalarRecord("val/loss"))
manager.add_record(MaxScalarRecord("train/accuracy"))
manager.add_record(MaxScalarRecord("val/accuracy"))

# get_record raises KeyError for a key that is not registered. To create the
# records on demand, pass a factory: RecordManager(default_factory=MinScalarRecord)

# Add values to each record
manager.get_record("train/loss").add_value(train_loss, step=epoch)
manager.get_record("val/loss").add_value(val_loss, step=epoch)
manager.get_record("train/accuracy").add_value(train_acc, step=epoch)
manager.get_record("val/accuracy").add_value(val_acc, step=epoch)

# Get the best values and the last values for logging
best_values = manager.get_best_values(prefix="best/")
last_values = manager.get_last_values(prefix="last/")

get_best_values skips the empty records and the records that are not comparable, and get_last_values skips the empty records. The same functions exist for any mapping of records: minrecord.get_best_values(records) and minrecord.get_last_values(records).

docs.title: Pattern 3: Early Stopping
docs.text:
from minrecord import MinScalarRecord

val_loss = MinScalarRecord("val_loss")
patience = 5

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    # Training...
    val_loss.add_value(epoch_val_loss, step=epoch)

    if val_loss.has_improved():
        save_checkpoint(model, "best_model.pt")

    # The count is derived from the best pair, so it survives to_dict/from_dict.
    # It needs a numeric step.
    if epoch - val_loss.get_best_step() >= patience:
        print(f"Early stopping at epoch {epoch}")
        break

docs.title: Pattern 4: Custom Comparators
docs.text:
For specialized metrics, create custom comparators:

from minrecord import ComparableRecord
from minrecord.comparator import BaseComparator


class F1Comparator(BaseComparator[tuple[float, float]]):
    """Maximize F1 score from precision and recall."""

    def is_better(self, *, new_value: tuple[float, float], old_value: tuple[float, float]) -> bool:
        def f1(p, r):
            return 2 * p * r / (p + r) if (p + r) > 0 else 0

        return f1(*new_value) >= f1(*old_value)


record = ComparableRecord("f1_components", F1Comparator())
record.add_value((precision, recall))

A comparator only implements is_better. The first value of a record is the best value, so the comparator does not need an initial value. The comparison must be reflexive: is_better(new_value=x, old_value=x) returns True for every x (a plateau is an improvement), as a record that is rebuilt from to_dict replays its last value against a best value that is that value. Use >= or <=, not > or <. If the comparator has some arguments, override to_dict so the record can be saved and loaded: {**super().to_dict(), "tolerance": self._tolerance}.

docs.title: Memory Usage
docs.text:
• Each record stores a fixed number of values (default 10)
  • Use max_size appropriately for your use case
  • Consider the size of each value (e.g., scalars vs large objects)

docs.title: Computational Cost
docs.text:
• Adding values is O(1) (deque append)
  • Getting best/last values is O(1)
  • Comparison operations depend on the comparator implementation

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Set appropriate max_size: Balance between memory and information needs
  2. Use RecordManager for multiple metrics to keep code organized
  3. Resume a run by saving manager.state_dict() (or record.to_dict()) in your checkpoint and loading it back
  4. Avoid storing large objects: Records store the values by reference and are meant for scalars or small objects

docs.title: PyTorch Example
docs.text:
import torch
from minrecord import MinScalarRecord, MaxScalarRecord

train_loss = MinScalarRecord("train_loss")
val_accuracy = MaxScalarRecord("val_accuracy")

for epoch in range(epochs):
    model.train()
    epoch_loss = 0
    for batch in train_loader:
        loss = train_step(model, batch)
        epoch_loss += loss.item()

    train_loss.add_value(epoch_loss / len(train_loader), step=epoch)

    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        acc = evaluate(model, val_loader)
    val_accuracy.add_value(acc, step=epoch)

    if val_accuracy.has_improved():
        torch.save(model.state_dict(), "best_model.pt")

docs.title: Logging Integration
docs.text:
import wandb
from minrecord import Record, RecordManager

# A record is created for every new metric name.
manager = RecordManager(default_factory=Record)

for epoch in range(epochs):
    # Training...
    # Add values to records
    for name, value in metrics.items():
        manager.get_record(name).add_value(value, step=epoch)

    # Log to wandb
    wandb.log(
        {
            "epoch": epoch,
            **manager.get_last_values(prefix="current/"),
            **manager.get_best_values(prefix="best/"),
        }
    )

docs.title: State Management
docs.text:
A record is saved with to_dict(): it is one flat dict with the arguments of the constructor (the full name of the class, the name, max_size, the recent values as elements and, for a comparable record, the comparator and the best pair as best). The dict can be written to JSON, if the values are numbers or strings.

>>> import json
>>> from minrecord import BaseRecord, MinScalarRecord
>>> record = MinScalarRecord("loss", max_size=2)
>>> record.update([(0, 1.0), (1, 5.0), (2, 6.0)])
>>> record.to_dict()
{'_target_': 'minrecord.comparable.MinScalarRecord', 'name': 'loss', 'max_size': 2, 'elements': ((1, 5.0), (2, 6.0)), 'best': (0, 1.0)}
>>> new_record = BaseRecord.from_dict(json.loads(json.dumps(record.to_dict())))
>>> new_record.equal(record)
True
>>> new_record.get_best_value()
1.0

from_dict creates a new record, with the validation of the constructor. load_dict loads the dict in an existing record, in place, for the objects that other parts of your code hold. It builds the new record first, so the record is not changed if the dict is invalid or if it is the dict of a record of another type:

record.load_dict(state)

Loading only builds records and comparators: a dict whose _target_ names another importable callable (for example collections.OrderedDict) raises TypeError before the callable is called. BaseRecord.from_dict accepts every record, and MinScalarRecord.from_dict only a MinScalarRecord (or a subclass). The module that _target_ names is still imported, so do not load a dict from an untrusted source without checking _target_ first.

For RecordManager:

# Save entire manager
manager_state = manager.state_dict()

# Load into new manager
new_manager = RecordManager()
new_manager.load_state_dict(manager_state)

The state of a manager is a dict of records dicts, so it can be written to JSON. load_state_dict merges the state into the manager: the data of a known key is loaded in the existing record (the objects that you hold are updated), the records of the new keys are created, and a record of the manager that the state does not mention is kept. It does not change the manager if one entry is invalid (the entries are built and checked first, then loaded). Two managers can be compared with manager1.equal(manager2) or coola.equality.objects_are_equal.

The dict is not compatible with the one of the versions before 0.4.0 ({"config": ..., "state": ...}), see the release notes. The design page explains the trade-offs of from_dict, load_dict and load_state_dict.

docs.title: Check if metrics are improving
docs.text:
record = MinScalarRecord("loss")
record.add_value(1.5)
record.add_value(1.3)
print(f"Has improved: {record.has_improved()}")  # True
print(f"Best value: {record.get_best_value()}")  # 1.3
print(f"Best step: {record.get_best_step()}")  # 1 if the best value was added with step=1

docs.title: Inspect recent history
docs.text:
print(f"Recent values: {record.get_most_recent()}")
print(f"Number of stored values: {len(record)}")

docs.title: Verify record equality
docs.text:
# Useful for testing
record1 = MinScalarRecord("loss", elements=[(0, 1.5), (1, 1.3)])
record2 = MinScalarRecord("loss", elements=[(0, 1.5), (1, 1.3)])
assert record1.equal(record2)

docs.title: minrecord.base.BaseRecord
docs.text:
Bases: ABC, Generic[T]

Define the base class to implement a record.

A record tracks the values added to it as well as the step when each value was added. The goal of this class is to keep the recent values in memory because the loggers (e.g. MLFlow or Tensorboard) do not allow to get the last value or the best value. The record keeps in memory a recent history of pairs (step, value) where step is the index of the step when the value was added (or None). The length of the recent history depends on the concrete implementation.

To implement your own record, you need to define the following members:

- ``name``
- ``add_value``
- ``get_last_value``
- ``get_most_recent``
- ``is_empty``
- ``to_dict``

The other methods are derived from them. clone, equal, update, from_dict and load_dict are @final, so a type checker rejects an override. A comparable record also overrides is_comparable, get_best_value, get_best_step and has_improved.

The contract of a record is:

1. ``to_dict`` returns exactly the arguments of the constructor
    that rebuild the record, including its content, and the
    full name of the class with the key ``_target_``. Thus
    ``BaseRecord.from_dict(record.to_dict()).equal(record)``.
2. The constructor accepts what ``to_dict`` returns, validates
    its arguments and raises before any object exists. The
    whole state of the record lives in ``vars(self)`` (no
    ``__slots__``), because ``load_dict`` replaces it.
3. ``get_best_value``, ``get_best_step`` and ``has_improved`` raise
    ``NotAComparableRecordError`` if the record is not
    comparable, and ``EmptyRecordError`` if the record is
    comparable and empty.

The values are stored by reference: to_dict and clone share the value objects with the original record. A record is not thread-safe.

Example 
>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("loss")
>>> record.add_value(value=2, step=0)
>>> record.add_value(value=1.2, step=1)
>>> record.get_last_value()
1.2

load_dict(data: dict[str, Any]) -> None

Load a dictionary in the current record, in place.

The new record is built first from the dictionary (with BaseRecord.from_dict), so the record is not modified if the dictionary is invalid.

The dictionary is the whole state of the record: the record takes its name, its max_size and its elements, and every attribute of vars(self) is replaced. Thus the state of a custom record must live in vars(self) (no __slots__). A caller that needs the name to stay the same checks it before.

required

Example 
>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("loss")
>>> record.load_dict(Record("loss", elements=[(0, 42.0)]).to_dict())
>>> record.get_last_value()

docs.title: minrecord.comparable.ComparableRecord
docs.text:
Bases: Record[T]

Implement a record of comparable values.

The best value is stored apart from the recent values: it is kept when the pair (step, value) that produced it leaves the recent values. The first value added to the record is the best value. A value that is equal to the best value counts as an improvement. The first value is compared with itself, so a value that the comparator cannot compare is rejected by add_value and the record stays empty.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

The name of the record.

required comparator BaseComparator[T] | dict[str, Any]

The comparator to use to find the best value, or its dictionary (the output of comparator.to_dict()).

required elements Iterable[tuple[float | None, T]]

The initial elements. Each element is a tuple with the step and its associated value. The elements are added with add_value, so the best value and the improvement flag are computed from them, and only the last max_size elements are kept.

() max_size int | None

The maximum number of elements to store in the record. If None, the default maximum size (see get_max_size) at the time of the creation of the record is used.

None best tuple[float | None, T] | None

The best pair (step, value) before the elements are added. It is useful when the best value is not in the elements anymore, because it has been removed from the recent values. It requires at least one element, because a record has a best value if and only if it has a value. None means there is no value yet.

None

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if name is not a str, or if comparator is a dictionary that is not the dictionary of a comparator (_target_ is missing, or it is not a BaseComparator).

ValueError

if max_size is not a positive integer, if best is not a pair (step, value), or if best is given without elements.

Example 
>>> from minrecord import ComparableRecord
>>> from minrecord.comparator import MaxScalarComparator
>>> record = ComparableRecord("value", MaxScalarComparator())
>>> record.add_value(64.0)
>>> record.add_value(42.0)
>>> record.get_last_value()
42.0
>>> record.get_most_recent()
((None, 64.0), (None, 42.0))
>>> record.get_best_value()
64.0

docs.title: minrecord.comparator.BaseComparator
docs.text:
Bases: ABC, Generic[T]

Define the base comparator class to implement a comparator.

To implement your own comparator, you only need to define the is_better method. A comparator that has some arguments needs to override to_dict too, so the comparator can be re-created and compared.

The comparison must be reflexive: is_better(new_value=x, old_value=x) returns True for every value x. A record relies on it to rebuild itself from to_dict.

Example 
>>> from minrecord import MinScalarComparator
>>> comparator = MinScalarComparator()
>>> comparator.is_better(old_value=0.4, new_value=0.6)
False

get_best_values(
    records: Mapping[str, BaseRecord[Any]],
    *,
    prefix: str = "",
    suffix: str = "",
) -> dict[str, Any]

Get the best value of each record.

This function ignores the empty and non-comparable records.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default records Mapping[str, BaseRecord[Any]]

The records and their associated keys.

required prefix str

The prefix used to create the dict of best values. The goal of this prefix is to generate a name which is different from the record name to avoid confusion. By default, the returned dict uses the same name as the record.

'' suffix str

The suffix used to create the dict of best values. The goal of this suffix is to generate a name which is different from the record name to avoid confusion. By default, the returned dict uses the same name as the record.

''

Returns:

Type Description dict[str, Any]

The dict with the best value of each record.

Example 
>>> from minrecord import (
...     MinScalarRecord,
...     MaxScalarRecord,
...     get_best_values,
... )
>>> record1 = MinScalarRecord("loss", elements=[(None, 1.9), (None, 1.2)])
>>> record2 = MaxScalarRecord("accuracy", elements=[(None, 42), (None, 35)])
>>> get_best_values({"loss": record1, "accuracy": record2})
{'loss': 1.2, 'accuracy': 42}
>>> get_best_values({"loss": record1, "accuracy": record2}, prefix="best/")
{'best/loss': 1.2, 'best/accuracy': 42}
>>> get_best_values({"loss": record1, "accuracy": record2}, suffix="/best")

Implement a simple record manager.

The manager stores records by key (by default, the name of the record) and gives the operations that work on all of them: the best values, the last values, and saving and loading the whole group. It can hold different types of records (Record, MinScalarRecord, custom records, ...). A manager is not thread-safe, and an empty manager is falsy because it defines __len__.

This class proposes an approach to manage a group of records, but it is possible to use other approaches. If this class does not fit your needs, feel free to use another approach.

Name Type Description Default records Mapping[str, BaseRecord[Any]] | None

The initial records to add to the manager. The mapping is copied, so adding a record to the manager does not change it.

None default_factory Callable[[str], BaseRecord[Any]] | None

>>> manager.add_record(MinScalarRecord("loss"))

>>> manager = RecordManager(default_factory=MinScalarRecord)
>>> manager.get_record("new_record")
MinScalarRecord(name=new_record, max_size=10, size=0)

load_state_dict(state_dict: dict[str, Any]) -> None

Load the state values from a dict.

The state is merged into the manager. The data of a key that is already in the manager is loaded in the existing record (load_dict), so the objects that other parts of the code hold are updated. The data of a new key creates a new record (BaseRecord.from_dict). A record of the manager that the state does not mention is kept. The manager is not modified if one entry is invalid.

The data of every entry is first validated by building a record with BaseRecord.from_dict. The data of a key that is already in the manager is then loaded with load_dict, which builds the record again, so an existing key is built twice. The cost is one more constructor call for a window of at most max_size pairs.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default state_dict dict[str, Any]

A dict with the new state values. It has the structure of the output of state_dict.

required

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if the data of a key is the data of a record of another type than the existing record, or if it is not the data of a record.

Example 
>>> from minrecord import RecordManager, Record
>>> manager = RecordManager()
>>> manager.add_record(Record("value"))
>>> manager.load_state_dict(
...     {
...         "value": {
...             "_target_": "minrecord.generic.Record",
...             "name": "value",
...             "max_size": 10,
...             "elements": ((0, 1), (1, 0.5), (2, 0.25)),
...         }
...     }
... )
>>> manager.get_record("value").get_last_value()

docs.title: minrecord
docs.text:
Root package.

minrecord is a minimalist library to record values in a machine learning workflow. Every record keeps at most max_size recent values, keeps the best value apart from them, is rebuilt exactly from to_dict, and only loads objects of the expected type. See the guarantees and the design choices in the design page of the documentation.

The public objects are:

  • records: Record (recent values), ComparableRecord, MinScalarRecord and MaxScalarRecord (recent values and best value), and the base class BaseRecord;
  • comparators: BaseComparator, MinScalarComparator and MaxScalarComparator, which define what a better value is;
  • RecordManager, get_best_values and get_last_values to work on a group of records;
  • get_max_size, set_max_size and reset_max_size for the default max_size;
  • EmptyRecordError and NotAComparableRecordError.

docs.title: minrecord.BaseRecord
docs.text:
Bases: ABC, Generic[T]

Define the base class to implement a record.

A record tracks the values added to it as well as the step when each value was added. The goal of this class is to keep the recent values in memory because the loggers (e.g. MLFlow or Tensorboard) do not allow to get the last value or the best value. The record keeps in memory a recent history of pairs (step, value) where step is the index of the step when the value was added (or None). The length of the recent history depends on the concrete implementation.

To implement your own record, you need to define the following members:

- ``name``
- ``add_value``
- ``get_last_value``
- ``get_most_recent``
- ``is_empty``
- ``to_dict``

The other methods are derived from them. clone, equal, update, from_dict and load_dict are @final, so a type checker rejects an override. A comparable record also overrides is_comparable, get_best_value, get_best_step and has_improved.

The contract of a record is:

1. ``to_dict`` returns exactly the arguments of the constructor
    that rebuild the record, including its content, and the
    full name of the class with the key ``_target_``. Thus
    ``BaseRecord.from_dict(record.to_dict()).equal(record)``.
2. The constructor accepts what ``to_dict`` returns, validates
    its arguments and raises before any object exists. The
    whole state of the record lives in ``vars(self)`` (no
    ``__slots__``), because ``load_dict`` replaces it.
3. ``get_best_value``, ``get_best_step`` and ``has_improved`` raise
    ``NotAComparableRecordError`` if the record is not
    comparable, and ``EmptyRecordError`` if the record is
    comparable and empty.

The values are stored by reference: to_dict and clone share the value objects with the original record. A record is not thread-safe.

Example 
>>> from minrecord import Record
>>> record = Record("loss")
>>> record.add_value(value=2, step=0)
>>> record.add_value(value=1.2, step=1)
>>> record.get_last_value()
1.2

docs.text:
Bases: Record[T]

Implement a record of comparable values.

The best value is stored apart from the recent values: it is kept when the pair (step, value) that produced it leaves the recent values. The first value added to the record is the best value. A value that is equal to the best value counts as an improvement. The first value is compared with itself, so a value that the comparator cannot compare is rejected by add_value and the record stays empty.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

The name of the record.

required comparator BaseComparator[T] | dict[str, Any]

The comparator to use to find the best value, or its dictionary (the output of comparator.to_dict()).

required elements Iterable[tuple[float | None, T]]

The initial elements. Each element is a tuple with the step and its associated value. The elements are added with add_value, so the best value and the improvement flag are computed from them, and only the last max_size elements are kept.

() max_size int | None

The maximum number of elements to store in the record. If None, the default maximum size (see get_max_size) at the time of the creation of the record is used.

None best tuple[float | None, T] | None

The best pair (step, value) before the elements are added. It is useful when the best value is not in the elements anymore, because it has been removed from the recent values. It requires at least one element, because a record has a best value if and only if it has a value. None means there is no value yet.

None

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if name is not a str, or if comparator is a dictionary that is not the dictionary of a comparator (_target_ is missing, or it is not a BaseComparator).

ValueError

if max_size is not a positive integer, if best is not a pair (step, value), or if best is given without elements.

Example 
>>> from minrecord import ComparableRecord
>>> from minrecord.comparator import MaxScalarComparator
>>> record = ComparableRecord("value", MaxScalarComparator())
>>> record.add_value(64.0)
>>> record.add_value(42.0)
>>> record.get_last_value()
42.0
>>> record.get_most_recent()
((None, 64.0), (None, 42.0))
>>> record.get_best_value()
64.0

docs.title: minrecord.RecordManager
docs.text:
Implement a simple record manager.

The manager stores records by key (by default, the name of the record) and gives the operations that work on all of them: the best values, the last values, and saving and loading the whole group. It can hold different types of records (Record, MinScalarRecord, custom records, ...). A manager is not thread-safe, and an empty manager is falsy because it defines __len__.

This class proposes an approach to manage a group of records, but it is possible to use other approaches. If this class does not fit your needs, feel free to use another approach.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default records Mapping[str, BaseRecord[Any]] | None

The initial records to add to the manager. The mapping is copied, so adding a record to the manager does not change it.

None default_factory Callable[[str], BaseRecord[Any]] | None

The function that creates the record of a key that is not registered. It is called with the key and must return a record. If None, get_record raises KeyError for an unknown key. The factory is not part of the state of the manager (state_dict, equal).

None Example 
>>> from minrecord import RecordManager, MinScalarRecord
>>> manager = RecordManager()
>>> manager.add_record(MinScalarRecord("loss"))
>>> manager.get_record("loss")
MinScalarRecord(name=loss, max_size=10, size=0)
>>> manager = RecordManager(default_factory=MinScalarRecord)
>>> manager.get_record("new_record")
MinScalarRecord(name=new_record, max_size=10, size=0)

load_state_dict(state_dict: dict[str, Any]) -> None

Load the state values from a dict.

The state is merged into the manager. The data of a key that is already in the manager is loaded in the existing record (load_dict), so the objects that other parts of the code hold are updated. The data of a new key creates a new record (BaseRecord.from_dict). A record of the manager that the state does not mention is kept. The manager is not modified if one entry is invalid.

The data of every entry is first validated by building a record with BaseRecord.from_dict. The data of a key that is already in the manager is then loaded with load_dict, which builds the record again, so an existing key is built twice. The cost is one more constructor call for a window of at most max_size pairs.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default state_dict dict[str, Any]

A dict with the new state values. It has the structure of the output of state_dict.

required

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if the data of a key is the data of a record of another type than the existing record, or if it is not the data of a record.

Example 
>>> from minrecord import RecordManager, Record
>>> manager = RecordManager()
>>> manager.add_record(Record("value"))
>>> manager.load_state_dict(
...     {
...         "value": {
...             "_target_": "minrecord.generic.Record",
...             "name": "value",
...             "max_size": 10,
...             "elements": ((0, 1), (1, 0.5), (2, 0.25)),
...         }
...     }
... )
>>> manager.get_record("value").get_last_value()
0.25
